--- title: Polars from Python and R subtitle: 'Pro-tip: Just swap `.` (Python) for `$` (R), or vice versa' execute: freeze: auto cache: true --- ## Load libraries ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import polars as pl import time import matplotlib ``` ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(polars) ``` ::: ::: ## Scan data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} nyc = pl.scan_parquet("nyc-taxi/**/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=True) nyc ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

NAIVE QUERY PLAN

run LazyFrame.show_graph() to see the optimized version

``` ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nyc = pl$scan_parquet("nyc-taxi/**/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=TRUE) nyc ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: ::: ## First example Polars operations are registered as queries until they are collected. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} q1 = ( nyc .group_by(["passenger_count"]) .agg([ pl.mean("tip_amount")#.alias("mean_tip") ## alias is optional ]) .sort("passenger_count") ) q1 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

NAIVE QUERY PLAN

run LazyFrame.show_graph() to see the optimized version

``` ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} q1 = ( nyc $group_by("passenger_count") $agg( pl$col("tip_amount")$mean()#$alias("mean_tip") ## alias is optional ) $sort("passenger_count") ) q1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: ::::{.callout-note} ## R-polars multiline syntax Polars-style `x$method1()$method2()...` chaining may seem a little odd to R users, especially for multiline queries. Here I have adopted the same general styling as Python: By enclosing the full query in parentheses `()`, we can start each `$method()` on a new line. If this isn't to your fancy, you could also rewrite these multiline queries as follows: ```r nyc$group_by( "passenger_count" )$agg( pl$col("tip_amount")$mean() )$sort("passenger_count") ``` :::: ::: (Note: this is the naive query plan, not the optimized query that **polars** will actually implement for us. We'll come back to this idea shortly.) Calling `collect()` enforces computation. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} tic = time.time() dat1 = q1.collect() toc = time.time() dat1 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

(Note that this next code chunk requires **graphviz**; see installation instructions [here](https://graphviz.org/download/).) ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # q2 # naive q2.show_graph() # optimized ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](polars-rpy_files/figure-html/pl_q2_show-1.png){width=1536} ::: ::: ### R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # q2 # naive cat(q2$explain()) # optimized ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SORT BY [col("passenger_count")] AGGREGATE[maintain_order: false] [col("tip_amount").mean().alias("mean_tip")] BY [col("month"), col("passenger_count")] FROM Parquet SCAN [nyc-taxi/year=2012/month=1/part-0.parquet, ... 2 other sources] PROJECT 3/24 COLUMNS SELECTION: [(col("month").cast(Float64)) <= (3.0)] ESTIMATED ROWS: 44907396 ``` ::: ::: ::: Now, let's run the query and collect the results. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ### Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} tic = time.time() dat2 = q2.collect() toc = time.time() dat2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## Appendix: Alternate interfaces The native **polars** API is not the only way to interface with the underlying computation engine. Here are two alternate approaches that you may prefer, especially if you don't want to learn a new syntax. ### Ibis (Python) The great advantage of **Ibis** (like **dbplyr**) is that it supports multiple backends through an identical frontend. So, all of our syntax logic and workflow from the Ibis+DuckDB section carry over to an equivalent Ibis+Polars workflow too. All you need to do is change the connection type. For example: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import ibis import ibis.selectors as s from ibis import _ ##! This next line is the only thing that's changed !## con = ibis.polars.connect() nyc = con.read_parquet("nyc-taxi/**/*.parquet") ( nyc .group_by(["passenger_count"]) .agg(mean_tip = _.tip_amount.mean()) .to_polars() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` shape: (18, 2) ┌─────────────────┬──────────┐ │ passenger_count ┆ mean_tip │ │ --- ┆ --- │ │ i64 ┆ f64 │ ╞═════════════════╪══════════╡ │ 9 ┆ 0.8068 │ │ 4 ┆ 0.844519 │ │ 66 ┆ 1.5 │ │ 6 ┆ 1.128365 │ │ 10 ┆ 0.0 │ │ … ┆ … │ │ 7 ┆ 0.544118 │ │ 177 ┆ 1.0 │ │ 208 ┆ 0.0 │ │ 65 ┆ 0.0 │ │ 249 ┆ 0.0 │ └─────────────────┴──────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} con.disconnect() ``` ::: ### tidypolars (R) The R package **tidypolars** ([link](https://www.tidypolars.etiennebacher.com/)) provides the "tidyverse" syntax while using **polars** as backend. The syntax and workflow should thus be immediately familar to R users. It's important to note that **tidypolars** is _solely_ focused on the translation work. This means that you still need to load the main **polars** library alongside it for the actual computation, as well as **dplyr** (and potentially **tidyr**) for function generics. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(polars) ## Already loaded library(tidypolars) library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE) library(tidyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE) nyc = scan_parquet_polars("nyc-taxi/**/*.parquet") nyc |> summarise(mean_tip = mean(tip_amount), .by = passenger_count) |> compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
